hookLine: The letter that follows will not say how to argue with it.

lines: HIS NAME WAS ON A TERRORIST LIST.
DID NOT SAY HOW TO ARGUE WITH IT.

OP.quote: Ramirez's wife had to purchase the car in her own name.
OP.attribution: TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, 594 U.S. 413 (2021) — SR-04

lines: WHO RECEIVED THE PIECE OF PAPER.

ACT_1.quote: On February 27, 2011, Ramirez visited a Nissan dealership in Dublin, California, seeking to buy a Nissan Maxima. Ramirez was accompanied by his wife and his father-in-law.
ACT_1.attribution: TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, 594 U.S. 413 (2021) — the Court's statement of facts (SR-01)

ACT_1.quote: ***OFAC ADVISOR ALERT - INPUT NAME MATCHES NAME ON THE OFAC DATABASE.
ACT_1.attribution: The alert carried on Ramirez's credit report, quoted at TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, 594 U.S. 413 (2021) — SR-02

ACT_1.quote: A Nissan salesman told Ramirez that Nissan would not sell the car to him because his name was on a 'terrorist list.'
ACT_1.attribution: TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, 594 U.S. 413 (2021), quoting the trial record at App. 333 — SR-03

events.text: The dealership. The car is not sold to him.
He requests his credit file. It arrives the same day — with no OFAC alert in it.
A second mailing arrives. The OFAC Letter.

ACT_1.quote: the name that appears on your TransUnion credit file 'SERGIO L RAMIREZ' is considered a potential match to information listed on the United States Department of Treasury's Office of Foreign Asset Control ('OFAC') Database.
ACT_1.attribution: The OFAC Letter, quoted in Ramirez v. TransUnion LLC, 951 F.3d 1008 (9th Cir. 2020) — SR-06

ACT_1.quote: Financial institutions are required to check customers' names against the OFAC Database, and if a potential name match is found, to verify whether their potential customer is the person on the OFAC Database. For this reason, some financial institutions may ask for your date of birth, or they may ask to a see a copy of a government-issued form of identification
ACT_1.attribution: The OFAC Letter's own instruction, quoted in Ramirez v. TransUnion LLC, 951 F.3d 1008 (9th Cir. 2020) — SR-07

ACT_1.label: Date of birth — the identifier the letter told institutions to ask for

ACT_1.quote: [OFAC records for the two prohibited SDNs who purportedly matched Ramirez, which include first, middle, and last names, dates of birth, and passport information]
ACT_1.attribution: Ramirez v. TransUnion LLC, 951 F.3d 1008 (9th Cir. 2020) — the court's bracketed description of what the letter enclosed, not the letter's own words (SR-08)

ACT_1.quote: Ramirez testified that he was confused by the two mailings. The lack of any OFAC information in the credit-report mailing suggested the alert had been removed, but the OFAC Letter mailing suggested otherwise.
ACT_1.attribution: Ramirez v. TransUnion LLC, 951 F.3d 1008 (9th Cir. 2020) — SR-09

ACT_1.quote: Ramirez also did not know how to remedy the issue because the OFAC Letter did not include instructions for initiating a dispute. Concerned about possible consequences of the OFAC match, Ramirez canceled an international vacation he had planned with his family.
ACT_1.attribution: Ramirez v. TransUnion LLC, 951 F.3d 1008 (9th Cir. 2020) — SR-10

ACT_1.quote: Concerned about the mailings, Ramirez consulted a lawyer and ultimately canceled a planned trip to Mexico. TransUnion eventually removed the OFAC alert from Ramirez's file.
ACT_1.attribution: TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, 594 U.S. 413 (2021) — SR-11

ACT_1.secondary: The Supreme Court writes 'a planned trip to Mexico'; the Ninth Circuit writes 'an international vacation … with his family'. Both are the record. Neither is merged into a third version. (SR-10, SR-11)

ACT_1.quote: Ramirez's credit report with the false OFAC alert was sent to a third party; Ramirez's alert stated that he was a match instead of a potential match; Ramirez was denied credit because of the alert; he canceled a vacation because of the alert; and he spent significant time and energy trying to remove the alert, including hiring a lawyer.
ACT_1.attribution: Ramirez v. TransUnion LLC, 951 F.3d 1008 (9th Cir. 2020) — SR-12

ACT_2.quote: As part of its enforcement efforts, OFAC publishes a list of individuals and companies owned or controlled by, or acting for or on behalf of, targeted countries. It also lists individuals, groups, and entities, such as terrorists and narcotics traffickers designated under programs that are not country-specific.
ACT_2.attribution: U.S. Treasury, Office of Foreign Assets Control — FAQ topic 1631 (LS-01)

ACT_2.quote: U.S. persons are prohibited from engaging in any transactions with SDNs and must block any property in their possession or under their control in which an SDN has an interest.

OFAC maintains a list of 'specially designated nationals' who threaten America's national security. Individuals on the OFAC list are terrorists, drug traffickers, or other serious criminals. It is generally unlawful to transact business with any person on the list.
ACT_2.attribution: TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, 594 U.S. 413 (2021) — LS-04

ACT_2.label: Records in Treasury's published sdn.csv dated 7 August 2026 — OUR count of Treasury's own file. Treasury publishes no current list size.

ACT_2.quote: Step 3. How much of the listed entry's name is matching against the name in your transaction? Is just one of two or more names matching (i.e., just the last name)? If yes, you do not have a valid match.
ACT_2.attribution: U.S. Treasury, OFAC — FAQ 5, the screener's own procedure (LS-06)

ACT_2.quote: Step 4. Compare the complete sanctions list entry with all of the information you have on the matching name in your transaction. … Are you missing a lot of this information for the name in your transaction? If yes, go back and get more information and then compare your complete information against the entry.
An entry often will have, for example, a full name, address, nationality, passport, tax ID or cedula number, place of birth, date of birth, former names and aliases.
ACT_2.attribution: U.S. Treasury, OFAC — what OFAC publishes for each entry (LS-08)

ACT_2.quote: A 'weak AKA' is a term for a relatively broad or generic alias that may generate a large volume of false hits when such names are run through a computer-based screening system.

It is merely a reminder to the person checking your credit that he or she should verify whether you are the individual on one of OFAC's sanctions lists by comparing your information to the OFAC information. If you are not the individual on the sanctions list, the person checking your credit should disregard the OFAC alert.
ACT_2.attribution: U.S. Treasury, OFAC — guidance for the consumer whose credit report carries an alert (LS-10)

ACT_2.quote: Beginning in 2002, TransUnion introduced an add-on product called OFAC Name Screen Alert.
ACT_2.attribution: TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, 594 U.S. 413 (2021) — LS-13

items.label: Identifiers OFAC publishes for each entry — name, address, nationality, passport, tax ID, place of birth, date of birth, former names, aliases
Identifiers TransUnion compared — first name, last name

ACT_2.quote: Accuity's software conducted a 'name-only' search, running a consumer's first and last name against the names on the OFAC list. A search would result in a match if the consumer's first and last name were either identical or similar to a name on the OFAC list (e.g., 'Cortez' would match with 'Cortes').
ACT_2.attribution: Ramirez v. TransUnion LLC, 951 F.3d 1008 (9th Cir. 2020) — LS-16

ACT_2.quote: Unsurprisingly, TransUnion's Name Screen product generated many false positives. Thousands of law-abiding Americans happen to share a first and last name with one of the terrorists, drug traffickers, or serious criminals on OFAC's list of specially designated nationals.
ACT_2.attribution: TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, 594 U.S. 413 (2021) — LS-15

ACT_2.quote: In collecting other types of data for use on consumer reports—such as tax liens or bankruptcy judgments—TransUnion used at least one additional identifier other than the consumer's name (e.g., address, date of birth, or social security number). OFAC information was the only consumer-report data that TransUnion collected using name alone.
ACT_2.attribution: Ramirez v. TransUnion LLC, 951 F.3d 1008 (9th Cir. 2020), footnote 2 — LS-17

ACT_2.quote: TransUnion presented no data showing that any of its name matches through OFAC Advisor were correct. In other words, TransUnion could not confirm that a single OFAC alert sold to its customers was accurate.
ACT_2.attribution: Ramirez v. TransUnion LLC, 951 F.3d 1008 (9th Cir. 2020), footnote 4 — LS-19

ACT_2.quote: When TransUnion first began offering the OFAC Advisor product, it determined that the OFAC alerts being placed on consumer credit reports were exempt from the FCRA
ACT_2.attribution: Ramirez v. TransUnion LLC, 951 F.3d 1008 (9th Cir. 2020) — the company's own legal position, as the court records it (LS-20)

ACT_3.quote: In 1970, Congress passed and President Nixon signed the Fair Credit Reporting Act.
ACT_3.attribution: TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, 594 U.S. 413 (2021) — MN-09

events.text: The Fair Credit Reporting Act — 'reasonable procedures to assure maximum possible accuracy'
TransUnion introduces OFAC Name Screen Alert
The OFAC Letters — 1 January to 26 July

ACT_3.primary: Cortez v. Trans Union, LLC, 617 F.3d 688 (3d Cir. 2010)
ACT_3.secondary: Recorded here only as Justice Thomas summarises it. The opinion itself was not retrieved, so nothing beyond his summary is said about it. (TH-04, open question ○-03)

ACT_3.quote: The report flagged her—Sandra Jean Cortez, born in May 1944—as a match for a person on the OFAC list: Sandra Cortes Quintero, born in June 1971.
ACT_3.attribution: Justice Thomas, dissenting — TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, 594 U.S. 413 (2021) — TH-04

ACT_3.quote: Most notably, the Third Circuit specifically reprimanded TransUnion for failing to use an additional identifier such as date of birth to verify the accuracy of OFAC matches.
ACT_3.attribution: Ramirez v. TransUnion LLC, 951 F.3d 1008 (9th Cir. 2020) — N9-02

ACT_3.quote: Plaintiffs presented evidence that—despite being told in 2010 by another circuit court that OFAC alerts were covered by the FCRA and subject to § 1681e(b)'s reasonable procedures requirement—TransUnion continued to utilize name-only searches to produce OFAC 'matches.'
ACT_3.attribution: Ramirez v. TransUnion LLC, 951 F.3d 1008 (9th Cir. 2020) — N9-01

ACT_3.quote: all natural persons in the United States and its Territories to whom TransUnion sent a letter similar in form to the March 1, 2011 [OFAC Letter] TransUnion sent to [Ramirez] . . . from January 1, 2011-July 26, 2011.
ACT_3.attribution: Ramirez v. TransUnion LLC, 951 F.3d 1008 (9th Cir. 2020) — the class definition (MN-01)

ACT_3.quote: TransUnion sent the same OFAC Letter to 8,184 other consumers who also requested copies of their credit reports between January 2011 and July 2011.
ACT_3.attribution: Ramirez v. TransUnion LLC, 951 F.3d 1008 (9th Cir. 2020) — SR-13

ACT_3.quote: In July 2011, TransUnion finally stopped sending OFAC Letters and began including OFAC alerts directly on the credit reports it sent to consumers.
ACT_3.attribution: Ramirez v. TransUnion LLC, 951 F.3d 1008 (9th Cir. 2020) — LS-21

events.text: The District Court rules all 8,185 have standing

ACT_3.label: Class members, including Ramirez — stipulated by both parties before trial
Of them, the members whose credit reports were disseminated to third parties between 1 January and 26 July 2011 — the same stipulation

ACT_3.quote: Ramirez and the class pursued only a willfulness theory for each of their three claims, presumably because statutory and punitive damages are available for willful, but not negligent, FCRA violations.
ACT_3.attribution: Ramirez v. TransUnion LLC, 951 F.3d 1008 (9th Cir. 2020) — MN-10

ACT_3.quote: At trial, Ramirez testified about his experience at the Nissan dealership. But Ramirez did not present evidence about the experiences of other members of the class.
ACT_3.attribution: TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, 594 U.S. 413 (2021) — SR-15

ACT_3.quote: After six days of trial, the jury returned a verdict for the plaintiffs. The jury awarded each class member $984.22 in statutory damages and $6,353.08 in punitive damages for a total award of more than $60 million.
ACT_3.attribution: TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, 594 U.S. 413 (2021) — MN-04

ACT_3.quote: We reduce the punitive-damages award from $6,353.08 per class member to $3,936.88 per class member, but otherwise affirm the verdict and judgment.
ACT_3.attribution: Ramirez v. TransUnion LLC, 951 F.3d 1008 (9th Cir. 2020) — the Ninth Circuit, before the case reached the Supreme Court (MN-06)

ACT_3.quote: Opinion by Judge Murguia; Partial Concurrence and Partial Dissent by
ACT_3.attribution: Ramirez v. TransUnion LLC, 951 F.3d 1008 (9th Cir. 2020) — Judge McKeown. The panel was not unanimous. (ID-07)

ACT_4.quote: To have Article III standing to sue in federal court, plaintiffs must demonstrate, among other things, that they suffered a concrete harm. No concrete harm, no standing.
ACT_4.attribution: TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, 594 U.S. 413 (2021) — the opening lines (HD-01)

ACT_4.primary: 25 June 2021 — TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, No. 20–297
ACT_4.secondary: JUSTICE KAVANAUGH delivered the opinion of the Court. On writ of certiorari to the United States Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit. (ID-01, ID-02)

ACT_4.label: Kavanaugh, Roberts, Alito, Gorsuch, Barrett — Thomas, Breyer, Sotomayor, Kagan

ACT_4.quote: Only plaintiffs concretely harmed by a defendant's statutory violation have Article III standing to seek damages against that private defendant in federal court.
ACT_4.attribution: TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, 594 U.S. 413 (2021) — the holding (HD-02)

ACT_4.quote: An injury in law is not an injury in fact.
ACT_4.attribution: TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, 594 U.S. 413 (2021) — HD-04

ACT_4.quote: The standing inquiry in this case thus distinguishes between (i) credit files that consumer reporting agencies maintain internally and (ii) the consumer credit reports that consumer reporting agencies disseminate to third-party creditors.
ACT_4.attribution: TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, 594 U.S. 413 (2021) — HD-06

ACT_4.quote: The mere presence of an inaccuracy in an internal credit file, if it is not disclosed to a third party, causes no concrete harm.
ACT_4.attribution: TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, 594 U.S. 413 (2021) — HD-07

ACT_4.quote: the plaintiffs' harm is roughly the same, legally speaking, as if someone wrote a defamatory letter and then stored it in her desk drawer. A letter that is not sent does not harm anyone, no matter how insulting the letter is. So too here.
ACT_4.attribution: TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, 594 U.S. 413 (2021) — the image the majority chose (HD-08)

ACT_4.quote: the risk of dissemination to third parties— was too speculative to support Article III standing
ACT_4.attribution: TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, 594 U.S. 413 (2021) — HD-09

items.label: 1,853 — the report went to a third party: standing
6,332 — the alert stayed in the internal file: no standing

ACT_4.quote: only 1,853 class members have standing for the reasonable-procedures claim and (ii) only Ramirez himself has standing for the two formatting claims relating to the mailings
ACT_4.attribution: TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, 594 U.S. 413 (2021) — HD-03

ACT_4.quote: We reverse the judgment of the U. S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit and remand the case for further proceedings consistent with this opinion.
ACT_4.attribution: TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, 594 U.S. 413 (2021) — HD-12

ACT_4.quote: the plaintiffs did not present any evidence that the 6,332 class members even knew that there were OFAC alerts in their internal TransUnion credit files. If those plaintiffs prevailed in this case, many of them would first learn that they were 'injured' when they received a check compensating them for their supposed 'injury.'
ACT_4.attribution: TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, 594 U.S. 413 (2021) — the majority's sharpest point (HD-10)

ACT_5.quote: TransUnion generated credit reports that erroneously flagged many law-abiding people as potential terrorists and drug traffickers.
ACT_5.attribution: Justice Thomas, dissenting — TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, 594 U.S. 413 (2021) — TH-01

ACT_5.quote: Yet despite Congress' judgment that such misdeeds deserve redress, the majority decides that TransUnion's actions are so insignificant that the Constitution prohibits consumers from vindicating their rights in federal court. The Constitution does no such thing.
ACT_5.attribution: Justice Thomas, dissenting — TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, 594 U.S. 413 (2021) — TH-02

ACT_5.quote: TransUnion did not compare birth dates, middle initials, Social Security numbers, or any other available identifier routinely used to collect and verify credit-report data.
ACT_5.attribution: Justice Thomas, dissenting — TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, 594 U.S. 413 (2021) — LS-18, TH-03

ACT_5.quote: TransUnion could not confirm that a single OFAC alert sold to its customers was accurate.
ACT_5.attribution: Justice Thomas, dissenting — TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, 594 U.S. 413 (2021), quoting Ramirez v. TransUnion LLC, 951 F.3d 1008 (9th Cir. 2020) footnote 4 — TH-06, LS-19

ACT_5.quote: one need only tap into common sense to know that receiving a letter identifying you as a potential drug trafficker or terrorist is harmful. All the more so when the information comes in the context of a credit report, the entire purpose of which is to demonstrate that a person can be trusted.
ACT_5.attribution: Justice Thomas, dissenting — TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, 594 U.S. 413 (2021) — TH-05
Justice Thomas, dissenting — TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, 594 U.S. 413 (2021), on state court as the remaining forum — TH-08

ACT_5.quote: The Court here transforms standing law from a doctrine of judicial modesty into a tool of judicial aggrandizement. It holds, for the first time, that a specific class of plaintiffs whom Congress allowed to bring a lawsuit cannot do so under Article III.
ACT_5.attribution: Justice Kagan, dissenting — TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, 594 U.S. 413 (2021) — KG-01

ACT_5.quote: Congress is better suited than courts to determine when something causes a harm or risk of harm in the real world.
ACT_5.attribution: Justice Kagan, dissenting — TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, 594 U.S. 413 (2021) — KG-05

ACT_5.quote: But why is it so speculative that a company in the business of selling credit reports to third parties will in fact sell a credit report to a third party?
ACT_5.attribution: Justice Kagan, dissenting — TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, 594 U.S. 413 (2021) — KG-04
Justice Kagan, dissenting — TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, 594 U.S. 413 (2021), on the reports already sent to potential creditors — KG-06

lines: WHAT THE COURT DID NOT DECIDE:

ACT_5.primary: Not decided: certification, and the state courts
ACT_5.secondary: The Court held only that FEDERAL courts lack jurisdiction over the 6,332. Certification was left to the Ninth Circuit on remand, and Justice Thomas flags state court as the remaining forum. (ND-03, ND-04, TH-08)
The risk-of-future-harm discussion expressly reserves the injunctive case — a material risk can satisfy concreteness there. This was a suit for damages. (ND-05)

ACT_5.primary: Not decided: what anyone finally received
ACT_5.secondary: No document retrieved states a final recovery. The Supreme Court set no dollar figure of its own. (ND-06, MN-11)

ENDING.primary: The record this film stands on ends on 25 June 2021
ENDING.secondary: What happened on remand, whether the 1,853 ever recovered anything, whether the parties settled — no document retrieved says. (open question ○-04)

items.label: 1,853 whose reports went to a third party

ENDING.quote: But why is it so speculative that a company in the business of selling credit reports to third parties will in fact sell a credit report to a third party?
ENDING.attribution: Justice Kagan, dissenting — TransUnion LLC v. Ramirez, 594 U.S. 413 (2021) — the last word of the film (KG-04)

Every card above is an entry in EP67_ramirez_FACTS_LEDGER.v001.md; every `quote` payload is a row graded VERBATIM in that ledger and re-verifiable with episodes/PD-2026-067-ramirez/01_research/sources/verify_quotes.v001.py (74/74 green). The row id is printed at the end of each attribution, so any card can be checked against the ledger without a lookup table. Nothing in this block is read by any tool.

PLACEMENT. build_case_film_generic.build_figures() does not read a per-beat time: it spaces a section's payloads EVENLY inside the section window (dur 6.0s, 3.0s in HOOK/OP), reserving 3.0s at the head and 6.5s at the tail. ORDER and COUNT are the only placement controls, and both follow FILM_BIBLE v001 section 6, whose beats are already in narration order. The bible's clock times (A2-11 at 9:55 and so on) were written against a 1,760 s design; the delivered master is shorter, so those times are not reproduced here -- the even spacing inside each measured section window is.

BEAT COUNTS. episode_spec figure_beats_per_act is [13, 17] and every ACT is inside it: ACT_1 16, ACT_2 16, ACT_3 17, ACT_4 15, ACT_5 14 -- exactly the counts FILM_BIBLE section 6 declares for each act. HOOK 3, OP 2 and ENDING 6 are not acts and the floor does not apply to them.

SACRIFICIAL SLOTS. build_figures overwrites figures[0] and figures[-1] with the AI-disclosure lowerthird. HOOK[0] and ENDING[-1] are already that exact card, so no content beat is destroyed (EP65 lost its closing line this way).

ATTRIBUTION IS A HARD RULE HERE, not a courtesy. Ledger quarantine entry -06 forbids TH-01, TH-07 and KG-02 in the film's own voice. Every ACT_5 quote card names the dissenting justice in its attribution line, and TH-07 ('ill-gotten gains') is not used at all. No card states a holding without saying who held it.

THE THREE MONEY FIGURES NEVER TOUCH (quarantine -03, -04). ACT_3 carries the jury's $984.22 and $6,353.08 on one card (MN-04) and the Ninth Circuit's reduction to $3,936.88 on the next (MN-06), in that order and with the Ninth Circuit named. The Supreme Court set no dollar figure at all, and no card anywhere states one for it; the arithmetic ~$40.3M (MN-07) appears nowhere. ACT_5's last card says out loud that what anyone finally received is unstated.

IT WAS 5-4 (quarantine -01). ACT_4[2] is a votetally with all nine justices named, placed there as the MECHANISM against the single easiest error in this episode. It is the only vote card in the film.

THE COURT-STAFF SUMMARY IS NOT QUOTED (quarantine -14). 'TransUnion, aware that its practice was unlawful' is the most quotable line in the Ninth Circuit file and it is not on any card. ACT_3 carries N9-02 and N9-01 instead, which say the same thing in the court's own words.

NUMBERS. The only numerals asserted are 19,199 (LS-05, labelled as OUR count of Treasury's published file and never as a Treasury statement, per quarantine -11), 8,185 / 1,853 / 6,332 (MN-02, MN-03 -- all three stated by the opinion itself), the money figures above, the identifier counts 9 and 2 (LS-08 against LS-14), the dates, and 'nearly 25%' quoted as Kagan's phrase rather than converted to 22.6% (KG-06). No false-positive rate appears anywhere: none exists in any retrieved document (open question -07).
NO acttitle CARDS, following EP66. Every slot in this film is spoken for by a ledger row, and the bible's beat map has no title beats in it.

Only plaintiffs concretely harmed by a defendant's statutory violation have Article III standing to seek damages against that private defendant in federal court.
An injury in law is not an injury in fact.
